newsitem.title: INDIA: India court order stays auction of Gandhi letters.
newsitem.headline: India court order stays auction of Gandhi letters.

text.p: An Indian court on Thursday ordered a stay against the auction of nationalist leader Mahatma Gandhi's papers, which is scheduled to be held in London on November 14, a court official said.
The stay on papers, a collection of writings which was expected to fetch up to one million sterling ($1.6 million), was ordered by Justice Jayasimha Babu of Madras high court, in south India.

Babu ordered the three parties involved should not in any manner deal or part with the items in question until the court had given its verdict in the civil suit filed by the Navjivan Trust, which claims the papers' ownership.

The three parties are V. Kalyanam, the Madras-based collector of the Gandhi memorabilia, Phillips, the London auctioners and Easun Katir, the British representatives of a Hawaiian Hindu monastery, which was to receive the auction proceeds.
Kayanam's lawyer declined to answer the charges in the court, effectively accepting the order, court officials said.

The Navjivan Trust, founded by Gandhi in 1929, has said that according to Mahatma's will, it was the sole heir to all his published and unpublished writings, including handwritten drafts of letters, articles and speeches.

"Kalyanam, who claimed to be a secretary of the Mahatma between 1944 and 1948, had been in unlawful posession of many of Gandhi's writings, mainly handwritten drafts, for the past 50 years and he was about to compound the illegality by auctioning them," the trust said in a statement.

Some of Gandhi's aides have said that Kalyanam was not his personal secretary but a stenographer who kept the rough drafts of the letters he wrote. Kalyanam says he has proof he was Gandhi's secretary.
The Navjivan petition said Phillips had indulged in "serious violation" of the trust's copyright by reproducing, in its sales catalogue, parts of Mahatma Gandhi's memorabilia.
The collection of handwritten papers includes letters to Britain's wartime prime minister, Winston Churchill, and Louis Mountbatten, the last British viceroy of India.

Many of the 450 pages in Gandhi's handwriting are in a cheap notebook and others were written on the backs of used envelopes by the environmentally conscious leader, who led 350 million Indians in a non-violent campaign against British rule.
The papers, now in London, reveal Gandhi's anxieties in the months before India gained independence in 1947 and his distress at the sectarian conflicts that erupted on partition.
Kalyanam had earlier asked Philips to postpone the auction following pressure from the Indian government not to sell Gandhi's letters.
